lines.text: as good; the claimful spirit of self-seeking and envy masks
itself as the requirement of justice when in fact, instead of the
right principle "No one should be worse off than I myself"
is set up the false principle "No one should be better off than
I myself"! Such is the language of self-seeking and envy.
And this selfish envious spirit is too easily inclined to
forget that it is impossible to establish complete equality
among men, that there will always be diversities among them
which are quite simply grounded in the diversity of human
endowment, gifts, and powers, and that no human organiza-
tional technique is capable of eliminating the differences
which fate decrees. But the mystery of our destiny lies in the
hands of God. And we often make the mistake of requiring
from God what we should require from ourselves as regards
the structural arrangements of human society. This we do
when we compare ourselves with others and feel discontented
because they are faring better than ourselves. Such behaviour
is the mean and envious behaviour of the labourers in the
parable. What this parable requires of us is freedom from
envy, and the capacity to rejoice in the good which others
enjoy. In point of fact we cannot for the most part make a
true judgment as to whether others are really better off than
ourselves. We see the outward aspect of things and we often
do not see how much inner sorrow and distress may be
concealed beneath a fair outward show.
And finally we forget so very easily that all the craft and the
effort involved in human organizing is in vain without the
blessing of God: "Unless the Lord builds the house, those
who build it labour in vain. Unless the Lord watches over
the city, the watchman stays awake in vain" (Ps. 127: 1).
Immersed as we are in our work and our effort to achieve
things, we forget that God's sovereign freedom also controls
and disposes our human exertions and that in His freedom
He can bring our work to prosperity, or lay it in ruins. And
so long as we are faring well, we tend to ascribe our pros-
perity to our own skill and ability, and blind ourselves to
God's goodness which wills to encounter and confront us both
in prosperity and adversity.
